---
title: "Exercises — Attaching a handle: the five ways"
---

Pen and paper. Try each problem before opening the **Hint**, and the hint before the **Solution**.

Have the [NEB selection charts](https://www.neb.com/en/tools-and-resources/selection-charts) open for the enzyme questions.

# Part 1 — Choosing a way

## E1. Pick the way

For each sample, pick the way of attaching a handle and say which property of the material decides it:

a. 2 ng of human genomic DNA, intact, and the result is wanted the same day.
b. 5 µg of human genomic DNA, sheared, and no PCR is wanted.
c. 10 pg of total RNA from a single human cell, with full-length transcripts wanted.
d. Total RNA from human plasma, mostly 20–30 nt.
e. 10 ng of ancient or heavily degraded DNA, partly single-stranded.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Ask: is the starting molecule DNA or RNA, how much is there, and how long is it? Does the method need the end to be free?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. Transposition. Tagmentation works from nanogram amounts and combines cutting and tagging in one step.
b. Ligation with a PCR-free workflow: repair, A-tail, ligate. A transposase would need amplification to finish the adapters.
c. RT with template switching. It adds the handle at the 5' end of the cDNA without a ligation, which is inefficient at this amount.
d. RNA ligation: a 3' pre-adenylated adapter then a 5' adapter. Short RNAs are too short for random priming to work well and have free ends.
e. Single-strand ligation or tailing. The molecules are too damaged for duplex end repair and A/T ligation. See the end-chemistry deck.
:::

## E2. What did the handle come from?

In [SMART-seq2](https://henriksson-lab.github.io/NGS_101/smart-seq2__10.1038+nmeth.2639/smart-seq2.html) the final library has an adapter at each end. List the ways by which handles were added across the whole protocol.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
- RT primer tail: the oligo-dT primer carries a known sequence that ends up at the 3' end of the cDNA.
- Template switching: the TSO provides the handle at the other end.
- Primer tails again: the PCR primers match those two handles.
- Transposition: Tn5 adds the sequencing adapters to the amplified cDNA.

Four steps, three of the five ways.
:::

# Part 2 — Ligation

## E3. Why an A and a T?

You have sheared DNA that is end-repaired, with a blunt-ended adapter available. Give two things that will happen in the tube and one thing that will not, if you do not A-tail the insert.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Inserts ligate to each other, giving chimeric molecules. Adapters ligate to each other and give dimers. Insert-adapter ligation happens too, but it competes with both. What will not happen is selection for the desired joint: a blunt ligase does not distinguish. With an A on the insert and T on the adapter, an A cannot pair with an A and a T cannot pair with a T.
:::

## E4. A half-useful library

You make a library with two different adapters, A and B, mixed in equal amounts. What fraction of the product has the right combination and what happens to the rest? What design avoids the loss?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Each end is independently A or B. Count the four cases.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Four equally likely combinations: AA, AB, BA and BB. Half carry both handles. The rest have the same handle at both ends and cannot be sequenced. A forked (Y) adapter provides both arms at each end, so every molecule has the pair of different handles after the first copy.
:::

# Part 3 — RNA ligation

## E5. A dimer instead of a library

A small-RNA library gives a strong band at about 120 bp and almost nothing at the insert size. Suggest the cause and say which reagent to change.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Which two oligos could ligate to each other in the second reaction?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Too much 3' adapter, or too little RNA. Free 3' adapter has a 5' end that the 5' adapter can use, so the two ligate. Reduce adapter, or remove free adapter before the 5' step. A smaller RNA input also makes this worse. Size selection afterwards removes the dimer.
:::

## E6. The trap of ATP

A 3'-blocked, pre-adenylated adapter is meant to be ligated to RNA with a 5'-P and a 3'-OH. A colleague swaps the truncated RNA ligase 2 for full-length T4 RNA ligase 1 and keeps ATP in the buffer. What new products can form?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Which ends on the RNA are now usable by an ATP-dependent enzyme?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
An ATP-dependent ligase can use the RNA's own 5'-P and 3'-OH. RNA molecules can circularise or join into concatemers, and neither takes up the adapter. The 3' block and the 5'-App on the adapter stop adapter-adapter joins, but they do not protect the RNA. Leaving ATP out and using the truncated enzyme is the design that prevents this.
:::

# Part 4 — Tailing and switching

## E7. Where did the junk reads come from?

A template-switching library has many reads that start with the TSO sequence followed by the middle of a gene. Give two explanations.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
The TSO can pair with internal runs of C or G and give the handle in the middle of a transcript. Premature RT stops are another plausible source: if RT falls off inside the transcript, the switch can happen there. Either way a read that starts at the TSO is not proof of a transcription start.
:::

## E8. Fixing a noisy amplicon library

You amplify an exon with 60-nt primers that carry both an index and P5/P7. Many reads are primer dimers. Redesign the PCR.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Use two steps. In step 1 use the gene-specific primers with short universal tails for a few cycles. Clean up with beads. In step 2 use universal primers carrying the index and P5/P7. The long primers never meet a gene-specific sequence, so they cannot mispair with each other through one.
:::

# Self-check

1. Name the five ways of attaching a handle.
2. What does a primer tail add, and what does it not change?
3. Why is the transposase's cut not always productive?
4. Why does a pre-adenylated adapter need no ATP?
5. What is the purpose of a forked adapter?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answers
1. DNA ligation, RNA ligation, primer tails, transposition, template switching.
2. It adds sequence at the 5' end of the product; the annealing part still decides specificity.
3. Both ends of a fragment are independent. A fragment with the same adapter at both ends does not amplify as well.
4. The AMP is already attached to the adapter's 5' end, which provides the energy for the joint.
5. Different arms at each end, from a single oligo pair.
:::
